title: I Own It. But Can I Prove It? How a Laptop Sale Took Me to the Police Station
excerpt: I knew the laptop was mine. I had bought it, repaired it, used it for years, and eventually decided to sell it. But when someone claimed it was their stolen laptop and the police became involved, I discovered an uncomfortable truth: owning something and proving you own it are two different things. Here's what happened and what I learned.
content:
## I Own It. But Can I Prove It? 
### The laptop was mine. I knew it was mine. The problem was proving it.
Most of us don't think much about proving that we own the used things we own.
You buy a used laptop. You use it for years. You repair it. You take photographs of it. Eventually, you decide to sell it.
Why would you need anything more?
I didn't think I needed anything more either.
Then, in August 2026, I found myself sitting at a police station trying to prove that a laptop I was selling actually belonged to me.
And that experience changed how I think about ownership.

---

## The laptop
On 18 August 2026, I listed a laptop for sale on Facebook Marketplace.
It wasn't anything unusual.
It was a clean listing, I had set a reasonable price, and I started receiving the usual messages from people interested in buying it.
The following day, everything changed.
A family had apparently had a laptop stolen the previous day.
They saw my Marketplace listing and became convinced that the laptop I was selling was theirs.
The husband contacted me and said he was interested in buying it.
We agreed to meet during lunch at a restaurant.
I left work, went home to collect the laptop, and went to meet him.
At that point, I thought I was meeting a potential customer.
I wasn't expecting the police to become involved.

---

## The strange check
When we met, I handed him the laptop and he started checking it.
That part wasn't unusual. If you're buying a used laptop, you should inspect it.
But something about the check was different.
He had a piece of paper with instructions on it, and I could see the word **CMD**.
At the time, I assumed he was simply checking the laptop thoroughly.
Later, I realised he may have been trying to obtain its serial number.
There was a problem, though.
He wanted to see the serial number on my laptop, but he hadn't brought his own serial number or any document showing the serial number of the laptop he claimed had been stolen.
The situation became increasingly uncomfortable.
Then the police arrived.
The DCI became involved, and suddenly I had gone from being someone selling a laptop to someone being treated as a potential suspect.

---

## At the police station
We went to the station so the matter could be investigated.
The person claiming the laptop was his tried to recover documents from the machine that he believed would prove his ownership.
That didn't work.
He then suggested that the hard drive had been thoroughly erased.
The officers asked me for the laptop's serial number.
Fortunately, I was able to retrieve it.
But there was another problem.
The person claiming the laptop was his had not produced a receipt, serial number, photograph, or other document connecting him to that particular machine.
His main evidence appeared to be that the laptop looked like the one he said had been stolen.
And that is when the situation really hit me.
### How do you prove that something belongs to you if you haven't kept evidence of that ownership?

---

## Fortunately, I had kept records
I had bought the laptop years earlier, in 2020.
Over the years, it had developed technical problems.
I repaired it gradually.
I had purchased replacement parts, including a motherboard, hard-drive connector and fan.
More importantly, I had kept records.
I had purchase records.
I had photographs.
I had videos of the laptop.
At the time, I hadn't created those records because I thought I'd one day have to defend myself at a police station.
I simply happened to have them.
That turned out to matter.

---

## The photographs became important
The next morning, I printed my documents and returned to the station.
I also had my family accompany me.
We went through the evidence.
Then we looked at photographs I had stored on my phone.
These were photographs of the same laptop that I had used in my Facebook Marketplace listing.
The photographs contained information (metadata) showing when they had been taken.
The dates were the deciding factor.
They were earlier than the date on which the other person's laptop had allegedly been stolen.
The officer compared the photographs with the physical laptop in front of us.
The machine matched.
Eventually, when the person claiming ownership saw the dates on the photographs, his position changed.
He accepted that it wasn't his laptop.
And that was the end of my role as the suspect.

---

## That experience left me with questions
What would have happened if I hadn't kept those photographs?
What if I had deleted them?
What if I had changed phones?
What if I had thrown away the purchase records?
What if I had simply said:
"Trust me. It's mine."
I don't know what would have happened.
And that's exactly the point.
After that experience, I started seeing things differently.
This led me to create the proof of purchase guide that contains all the necessary steps and tools that would prevent you from experiencing what I experienced that day at the police station.
